title: Trust, legal and governance (cross-cutting)
summary: The legal substance is unusually complete for a pre-launch product: consents are separate and unticked, every policy is dated, the controller is named, and export and deletion are in the product. The design does not yet let a member feel that. Trust facts sit in grey fine print, in documents and in FAQ accordions, while the moments that carry the most weight (the health-data consent, the pay step, the privacy controls) are the least explained. The one change that matters most: explain each trust moment in one plain sentence at the place where it is asked, starting with the health-data consent and the cancellation deadline next to the Pay button. References 13 and 14 (2026-11-21) prepare planned maintenance: a notice in advance with the exact window, and a status page that answers in one line. References 15 to 17 (2026-11-22) prepare the dashboard error page (slice 13.2): the error stays inside the app, 'Try again' works, there is a second way out and a reference to copy for support. References 18 to 33 (2026-11-23) prepare the trust centre and policy layout (slice D6.1) and the trust moments of the public site: the plain-language layer and contents on phones, acting on a right from the page that describes it, the cookie dialog, newsletter consent, who runs Eleva in the footer and on the contact page, the pay step and the accessibility statement.
strengths: Checkout consents are four separate, unticked checkboxes, and the AI and transcription choice is marked Optional and left off (04-booking-checkout/05-paid-step-details). Keep the separation; improve the explanation.

The details step turns the cancellation policy into dated facts for this booking: "Full refund if you cancel before 15 Nov 2026, 10:00" (04-booking-checkout/06-paid-details-filled). This is the best trust line in the funnel.

Every card on the trust index has a one-line plain description and a last-updated date, and the page ends with privacy@ and security@ contacts plus a vulnerability disclosure page (09-trust/01-trust).

The privacy notice has a last-updated date, numbered sections, a sticky contents list on desktop, a purposes and legal bases table, the controller's legal name, NIPC and address, and the route to complain to the CNPD (09-trust/02-legal-privacy).

Consents, data export and account deletion live on one Privacy page in the member sidebar, deletion has a 14-day waiting period, and marketing notifications are off by default (10-member-space/05-privacy, 10-member-space/06-settings).

The "Need urgent help?" block with 112, SNS 24 and the crisis lines appears where a health note is typed and again on the thank-you page (04-booking-checkout/09-free-thank-you). It reads as care, not as a disclaimer.

The product already says who provides care: the hero line "Eleva connects you with independent health experts who run their own practice", the profile questions "Who provides my care?" and "What does Eleva check?", and the registration-check line on the experts page.
The profile shows the professional body, licence number and ERS registration number, and the footer links the electronic complaints book and reopens cookie settings.

findings.title: The health-data consent is a bare link at the moment it is asked
findings.detail: The most sensitive choice in the product reads "I consent to health data processing", one of four identical grey rows under the heading "Policy and consent" and the intro "To book a health session on this digital health platform, please confirm:". Nothing on the screen says what health data means here, who sees it, or that the member can withdraw. The member has to leave a filled form and read a policy to find out. A woman booking pelvic health or fertility care wants that answer before she ticks. Consent that is given without understanding is also weaker consent: whether the label alone is specific and informed enough needs legal review. The note field "Anything you want the expert to know" sits a full card above the consent it depends on.
findings.recommendation: Keep four separate unticked boxes. Rename the card "Before you book" and open it with a short promise in Lora, for example "Your health details stay between you and your expert", followed by two plain lines: who sees what you write (the expert you book), and that you can withdraw in Privacy settings. Give each checkbox a bold short label and one grey line of explanation: "Health information. I agree that Eleva handles the health details in this booking so my expert can prepare. Read the health data notice." Open each notice in a sheet or dialog so the form is never lost. Move the consent card directly under the note field on mobile so cause and consent are read together. Final wording needs legal review.

findings.title: The Privacy page shows five teal "Grant" buttons and no record of what the member agreed to
findings.detail: The Consents card promises "See what you agreed to" but shows no status, no date and no on or off state. Each row (Terms of use, Privacy notice, Health data processing, Marketing messages, AI help) has the same primary "Grant" button and a raw "Version 2026-11-14". A member cannot tell whether health-data consent is active, cannot see how to withdraw it, and is nudged by a primary button to opt in to marketing. Terms of use and the privacy notice appear as things to grant, which mixes a contract and a notice with real consents; whether they belong in this list needs legal review. On mobile the five full-width buttons fill two screens before export and delete appear.
findings.recommendation: Turn the card into a status list in two groups. "Needed to use Eleva": Terms of use and Privacy notice as read-only rows with "Accepted 14 November 2026" and a "Read" link. "Your choices": Health information, Marketing messages, Live transcription, AI help with session reports, each with a switch, a one-line plain description, the date it was last changed, and the consequence of turning it off ("Turning this off cancels nothing you have booked. To stop a booked session, cancel it first."). Show the version as a date in words. A withdrawal uses the same single control as the grant.

findings.title: The cancellation deadline disappears at the pay step on mobile and is generic on desktop
findings.detail: The details step states the exact refund deadline. One step later, where the member pays, the mobile summary card shows only the service, time and hold timer: no cancellation terms at all. Desktop keeps one grey line, "Full refund if you cancel at least 24 hours before the session", without the date. The member commits money on the screen with the least information about getting it back. Showing the main terms, including cancellation, directly before the payment action is also a consumer-law expectation; the exact wording, and whether a withdrawal-right statement is required for a dated health service, needs legal review.
findings.recommendation: Carry the dated line into the summary card on both breakpoints, with an icon and normal text colour: "Free cancellation until Sun 15 Nov, 10:00. After that, no refund." with a "Cancellation policy" link that opens the full Flexible rules in a sheet. Repeat one short line directly under the Pay button: "By paying you confirm this booking and its cancellation policy." Use the same component on the thank-you page and in the confirmation email so the member reads one sentence three times.

findings.title: Credentials read as fine print and the explanation of what Eleva checks is at the bottom of the page
findings.detail: The strongest proof on a profile, "Ordem dos Fisioterapeutas · Licence no. … · ERS registration no. …", is one small grey line with no icon, no statement that Eleva checked it, and no date. The answer to "What does Eleva check?" is the sixth and last accordion, far below the booking card on mobile. Listing cards show no profession or registration at all, so with a missing photo a card is a monogram and a name. For a new marketplace with no reviews yet, verified registration is the main reason to trust a stranger with a health problem, and it is styled like a caption.
findings.recommendation: Add a "Registration checked" row in the header and repeat it in the booking card above the CTA: a shield-check icon, "Physiotherapist · Ordem dos Fisioterapeutas no. 12345", "Checked by Eleva in November 2026", and a "What we check" link opening a short popover (identity, professional body registration, ERS where it applies, how often it is rechecked). Link the number to the public register where the professional body offers one. On listing cards add the profession and a small checked mark under the name. Only claim what the verification process does; the label wording ("checked" versus "verified") needs legal review.

findings.title: The trust centre is an index of thirteen documents with equal weight
findings.detail: The page is two grids of identical white cards. A member who wants to know "is my health information safe here?" has to choose between Security, Data processing agreement, Sub-processors and Health data notice and then read a policy. The first card a member meets after Security is a contract written for experts and clinics. There are no facts on the page itself, no icons, no grouping by reader, and no word on who is behind Eleva. On mobile it is thirteen stacked cards, about 4,300 px, before the contact line.
findings.recommendation: Lead with proof, then documents. Under the heading add five or six fact tiles, each an icon, a specific claim and a link: who can read your session notes, where data is stored, how session records are encrypted, how expert registration is checked, how payments are handled, that sessions are not recorded. Then group the documents by reader with a short label each: "For members", "For experts and clinics", "Security researchers". Add a "Who runs Eleva" block (legal name, NIPC, address, regulator registration, privacy and security contacts) and a "Report a concern" entry. Keep the dated cards; they are good.

findings.title: The pay step does not say who provides the session, who is paid, or whether the price is final
findings.detail: The summary names "Fisio Mota" and a price, and the page is branded Eleva. Nothing at the point of contract says the session is delivered by an independent expert, that Eleva arranges booking and payment, or who issues the invoice. "Total" sits alone on a line with the amount on the next line and no tax note. The subheading "Card, Apple Pay, Google Pay, Link, and MB WAY may appear" sounds unsure. There is no line saying the card details go to Stripe. Platform transparency and total-price rules both point at this screen; the exact statements need legal review.
findings.recommendation: Add a provider line to the summary card: "Your session is with Fisio Mota, an independent physiotherapist. Eleva takes care of booking and payment, and your expert sends the invoice." Set the total as one row, label left and amount right, with "Taxes included" or the correct VAT wording beneath (needs legal review). Replace the subheading with "We hold your time while you pay." and add a lock line under the button: "Paid securely through Stripe. Eleva never sees your card number." All of this is copy around the Payment Element, not a change to it.

findings.title: Legal pages have no plain-language layer, no contents on mobile, and no way to act on a right
findings.detail: The privacy notice is well written but opens straight into "1. Who the controller is". There is no short summary for a member who will read thirty seconds. On mobile the page runs about 11,700 px with no contents list or jump links, and the two-column legal bases table squeezes into narrow columns. Section 8 tells members to write an email to use their rights, although export and deletion already exist in Privacy settings. Section 10 joins "Artificial intelligence and cookies", two unrelated topics. The DPO bullet describes an appointment still to come, which reads as something missing; how to state the current contact needs legal review.
findings.recommendation: Add an "In short" box under the title with five bullets (what we collect, who sees health information, where it is stored, how long, your choices) and the note that the full text below is what applies. On mobile add a collapsible "On this page" under the date and a back-to-top control; stack the table as purpose-then-basis cards. In "Your rights" add two buttons, "Download your data" and "Delete your account", that go to Privacy settings, plus a short request form for people who booked as guests. Split AI and cookies into two sections. State the data protection contact positively as the one address that reaches the right person. Apply the same template to every policy.

findings.title: Delete account is explained in internal terms and its safeguards are not visible
findings.detail: The explanation uses "Account-scope data", "Booking-scope consents", "de-identified", "retain-then-destroy rule" and "This cannot be shortened from this screen". A member cannot tell from this whether her session notes are deleted. The reassuring fact, a 14-day window to change her mind, is the last line. The button is a pale pink pill that looks disabled. The page does not suggest downloading data first, and the capture set has no confirmation step, so its design could not be judged. "Download your data" has no state for a request in progress or a past export.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite as two short lists. "What we delete": your profile, your sign-in, your notification and marketing choices. "What we keep, and why": session records, with your name removed, for the period Portuguese health-record rules require; payment records for tax law. Lead with "You have 14 days to change your mind". Offer "Download your data first" inside the delete card. Make the confirmation a dialog that repeats the consequences in one sentence, links the privacy notice, and uses an explicit button label such as "Delete my account". After a request, show a dated status row for export and for deletion with a "Cancel deletion" action. Retention statements need legal review.

findings.title: The optional AI choice bundles transcription and AI drafting in one long sentence
findings.detail: At checkout the fifth checkbox is a 45-word sentence covering two different things: live transcription of the call, and AI help with the expert's notes. It sits in the same list as the required boxes with only the word "Optional:" to set it apart, and on mobile it wraps to seven lines. In Privacy settings the same choice is a seven-line paragraph that ends with "AI drafting is not switched on yet", which tells the member about something Eleva does not do. A member cannot accept transcription and decline AI drafting. Whether one consent can cover both purposes needs legal review.
findings.recommendation: Lift it out of the required list into its own tinted block titled "Optional: a written record of your session". Use a switch, two short bullets (what is transcribed and who reads it; that your expert writes and checks the report), and the line "You can change this any time in Privacy settings." If the two purposes can run independently, offer two switches. Describe only what happens today. Add a visible notice in the call itself whenever transcription is on, with the same wording.

findings.title: There is no visible way to report a concern about an expert or a session
findings.detail: The profile has "Website" and "Share this page" but no "Report". The thank-you page has no "Something wrong?" route. The only path is the footer link to the complaints policy, which is a document, not an action. For a health marketplace, a member who sees a wrong credential or has a bad session needs a short, safe way to say so, and seeing that route exists is itself a trust signal. A notice route for listings is also expected of online platforms; scope needs legal review.
findings.recommendation: Add a quiet "Report a concern" link at the foot of every profile and on each session in the member Space. Open a two-step dialog: pick a reason (registration or identity, conduct in a session, payment or refund, something else), add details. State "Your expert will not see who sent this" where that is true, confirm with a reference number and the time to a reply, and link the complaints policy and the electronic complaints book. List the same route on the trust centre.

findings.title: The footer lists fourteen legal links and does not say who is behind Eleva
findings.detail: The Legal column runs from Terms to Cookie settings in one undifferentiated list, mixing member essentials with Expert agreement, Photo credits and Evidence-based care. The complaints book, which Portuguese members look for, is tenth. The bottom line reads "© 2026 Eleva.care. All rights reserved." with no legal name, registration number or address, so a visitor has to open the privacy notice to learn which company holds her data. On mobile the footer is longer than a screen and a half.
findings.recommendation: Split into two shorter columns: "Legal" (Terms, Privacy, Cookies, Payments and refunds, Complaints, Electronic complaints book) and "Trust" (Trust and security, Health data, AI, Accessibility, Cookie settings). Move Expert agreement under the professionals column and Photo credits to the bottom bar. Replace the copyright line with an identity line: legal name, NIPC, registered address, and the regulator registration where one applies. Show the official complaints-book mark if its use is required or permitted (needs legal review).

findings.title: Sign-up and checkout ask for the same agreements in different words
findings.detail: Sign-up with email uses one checkbox, "I agree to the Terms and Privacy Policy". Sign-up with Google uses a passive line, "By continuing with Google, you agree to…". Checkout uses two boxes, "I agree to the terms of use" and "I have read the privacy notice". The same documents have three names (Terms, terms of use, booking terms; Privacy Policy, privacy notice) and three mechanisms. A careful reader wonders whether these are different documents. Asking someone to "agree" to a privacy notice, and accepting by a tick on one path and by continuing on another, needs legal review.
findings.recommendation: Create one shared consent component in the UI package with fixed document names ("Terms of use", "Privacy notice") and fixed verbs (agree to the terms, have read the notice). Use it on email sign-up, Google sign-up and checkout. When a signed-in member who already accepted the current versions books, show a single quiet line, "You accepted the Terms of use and Privacy notice on 14 November 2026", and ask only for what is new: the health information consent and the adult confirmation.

findings.title: How experts are ordered is a small grey link under the results
findings.detail: "Before a profile goes live, our team checks the expert's professional registration. How we order experts" is one caption-sized grey sentence below the grid. Two different promises share it: verification, which is a selling point, and ranking transparency, which platform rules expect to be easy to find next to the ranked results. A member reads the cards first and will never reach it on mobile once there are more than three experts. Placement and content of the ranking explanation need legal review.
findings.recommendation: Split the two. Put the verification promise above the grid as a short line with a shield icon, linked to "What we check". Put "How we order experts" next to the results count or sort control at the top of the list, opening a popover that names the main factors in plain words and says whether payment affects order.

findings.title: The homepage trust strip lists benefits, not proof
findings.detail: "Independent experts · Online or in person · In your language · Clear prices" are four labels with icons and no link. None is a checkable fact. The two facts that would reassure a first-time visitor, that every expert's registration is checked and that health information is protected, live only on inner pages.
findings.recommendation: Make two of the four items proof with a destination: "Registration checked for every expert" linking to what Eleva checks, and "Your health information stays private" linking to the trust centre. Keep "Clear prices" and "Online or in person".

findings.title: The thank-you page names the cancellation policy but not the deadline or how to cancel
findings.detail: "Changes and refunds follow the Flexible cancellation policy" uses the internal tier name and gives no date and no action. A guest with no account does not know where she would cancel.
findings.recommendation: Reuse the dated line from checkout: "Free to change or cancel until Thu 10 Dec, 16:00" with "How to cancel" pointing to the link in the confirmation email.

findings.title: The cookie banner and preferences dialog are missing from the capture set
findings.detail: No capture shows the consent banner, so its design could not be judged. The source (packages/consent/src/consent-chrome.tsx) describes a compact bottom bar with both choices in one row and "Customize" as a text link on phones, which is the right shape. Equal visual weight for accept and reject, and the wording, still need a visual check and legal review.
findings.recommendation: Add first-visit captures of the banner and the preferences dialog on desktop and mobile. Check that accept and reject are the same size and style, that necessary cookies are labelled "Always on" and optional groups start off, and that the dialog can be confirmed with one button.

findings.title: The cookie dialog names each group but hides what it does behind a plus sign
findings.detail: The first-visit captures now exist (2026-11-14-d0.3), so TRUST-16 can be judged. The banner is the right shape: 'Reject optional' and 'Accept all' are the same size and style. In the preferences dialog the two groups are bare labels, 'Essential' and 'Newsletter sign-up', each behind a small plus. The descriptions Eleva has written (what essential cookies do, that the newsletter form comes from Beehiiv) stay hidden until a tap, so a visitor deciding on 'Newsletter sign-up' cannot see that it only shows a sign-up form. The locked Essential switch is told apart by a paler colour only. On the banner 'Customize' is greyer than the other two buttons and reads as switched off.
findings.recommendation: Show each group's one-sentence description under its name without a tap, and write 'Always on' beside the Essential switch. Give 'Customize' the same text colour as the other two choices. On the newsletter page, say beside the form what the member agrees to and who provides the form, so the choice is clear where it is made. In the cookie policy, put a 'Cookie settings' button where withdrawal is described. Wording needs legal review.

references.pattern: Separate health-data consents under a human promise
references.why: A women's health app asks for three separate consents on one screen. It opens with "Your body. Your data" and a one-sentence promise about sharing and deletion, then each tick states its purpose in the label ("processing of my personal health data for providing me Flo app functions") with the policy link inline. The health consent is its own box, apart from terms.
references.apply: Open the checkout consent card with a short promise, keep each consent separate, and write the purpose into each label so the health-data box explains itself. The same component serves sign-up and checkout with one set of document names.
references.query: therapy app consent to process sensitive health information screen

references.pattern: Three plain promises before "I consent", including the AI disclosure
references.why: A bottom sheet for health data: a shield mark, the headline "Private by design", then three icon rows in everyday words: where queries go and that AI providers may not train on them, that data is encrypted and never sold, and that you can disconnect or delete at any time. Only then the "I consent" button and the policy link. Not a health marketplace; kept for how it explains health data and AI use in three lines.
references.apply: Use the three-row format above the health consent (who sees it, how it is protected, how to withdraw) and inside the optional AI block (what is transcribed, that the expert writes the report, how to turn it off).
references.query: therapy app consent to process sensitive health information screen

references.pattern: Dated cancellation deadline in the order summary at "Confirm and pay"
references.why: On the pay step the summary card leads with "Free cancellation. Cancel before Jul 14, 8:00 AM (WITA) for full refund", above date, guests and price details, with the total as one row. The agreement line with links to booking terms sits directly above the pay button.
references.apply: Carry Eleva's dated refund line into the pay-step summary on mobile and desktop, place the short agreement line by the Pay button, and reuse the same dated line on the thank-you page.
references.query: marketplace booking checkout with cancellation policy

references.pattern: The platform names who you are actually booking with, beside the total
references.why: The review step has a small card under the price summary: "KAYAK has partnered with CarRentals.com… You are booking directly with" followed by the provider's logo. The consent line above the button names both parties' terms. Price details list taxes and fees before the total. A travel product, kept for how it states the platform's role at the point of contract.
references.apply: Add a provider line to the pay-step summary that says the session is with the named independent expert and that Eleva handles booking and payment, and show the total with its tax note as one row.
references.query: marketplace booking checkout with cancellation policy

references.pattern: A check badge by the name and a plain line next to the CTA saying what the check covers
references.why: The carer's name carries a small shield badge. Directly above the contact button a shield row explains the check the platform requires for every carer, with "Learn more". A separate "Credentials" block states precisely what the platform does and does not confirm, so the badge claims no more than the process behind it.
references.apply: Put a "Registration checked" row with professional body and number next to the expert's name and in the booking card, with a "What we check" popover, and keep the claim exactly as wide as Eleva's verification.
references.query: healthcare marketplace provider profile with verified credentials

references.pattern: Proof tiles: one icon, one specific claim, one short explanation
references.why: Under "Protecting you and your money" each tile makes a single checkable statement (safeguarded with leading banks, licensed, audited regularly) with two lines of explanation and a link to the detail. A reader gets the facts without opening a document. A finance product, kept for the structure.
references.apply: Open the trust centre with five or six fact tiles about health information, storage, encryption, expert checks and payments, then list the dated documents grouped by reader. Use two of the same facts in the homepage trust strip.
references.query: trust and safety section on a marketplace site

references.pattern: Policy page with persistent contents and privacy-request actions at the top
references.why: The privacy policy keeps a full contents list in a fixed left rail and puts two buttons at the top right of the document: "View Past Requests" and "Make a Privacy Request". The effective date sits under the title. A reader can act on a right from the page that describes it.
references.apply: Add "Download your data" and "Delete your account" actions to the "Your rights" section and the top of the privacy notice, give mobile a collapsible contents list, and add an "In short" summary under the date.
references.query: privacy policy page with table of contents

references.pattern: Preference centre with equal "Reject All" and "Accept All", per-purpose switches and "Always Active"
references.why: The dialog puts "Reject All" and "Accept All" side by side at the same size. Each purpose is an expandable row with a switch and a plain description, the essential group is labelled "Always Active" instead of offering a fake choice, and one "Confirm" saves. A hiring marketplace, kept for the consent structure.
references.apply: Use this row model for the member Privacy page (required items shown as fixed, optional ones as switches with state) and check Eleva's cookie banner and dialog against it for equal accept and reject.
references.query: cookie consent banner with reject button

references.pattern: Privacy tab with access and deletion requests, each with a dated status history
references.why: One Privacy tab holds Cookies, "Access your data" and "Delete your data". After a request a banner confirms it and says how long it may take, and a history table shows the request date, whether the report is ready, and until when it can be downloaded. Deletion has its own status table. A storage product, kept for the request states.
references.apply: Give "Download your data" and "Delete account" a status row each: requested on, ready or scheduled for, link expires on, with "Cancel deletion" during the 14 days. Add a link to cookie settings on the same page.
references.query: privacy settings page with data export and delete account

references.pattern: "Manage my data" as four plain rights, then a delete confirmation that names the consequences
references.why: A women's health app turns data rights into a four-row menu, each with an icon and one sentence: Request information, Change account details, App consents, Delete my account ("including cycle and health-related data"). The delete alert says what is deleted, that you will be logged out, that it cannot be undone, and offers the privacy policy beside the destructive action and Cancel.
references.apply: Describe each privacy control in one member-facing sentence, state that deletion covers health information and what is kept, and give the delete confirmation an explicit label, the consequence in one sentence and a link to the notice.
references.query: deleting an account in a health app

references.pattern: Report a listing: short reason list, anonymity line, then a reference number and who reviews it
references.why: The report dialog asks for one reason from four radio options and says under the title "Your report will be kept anonymous". The last step gives a report ID, says the Trust and Safety team will review it, and points to support for follow-up. A freelance marketplace, kept for the flow.
references.apply: Add "Report a concern" to expert profiles and sessions with health-appropriate reasons, a confidentiality line, a reference number and a reply time, linked to the complaints policy and the electronic complaints book.
references.query: reporting a profile in a marketplace app

references.pattern: Footer that states who the company is, where it is registered and who regulates it
references.why: Beside the logo the footer gives the registered office, the line "Authorised and regulated by…", and regulator and certification marks. The bottom bar carries the registration and VAT numbers. Policies are a short column of three: Complaints, Privacy Policy, Terms. A law firm, kept for the identity block of a regulated service.
references.apply: Add an identity line to Eleva's footer (legal name, NIPC, registered address, regulator registration where it applies), shorten the legal column, and give the complaints book a clear place.
references.query: footer with company legal details

references.pattern: Status page that answers in one headline, then each service with its state and 30-day history
references.why: The page opens with a tick and one headline (here in German: all services are available), the time of the last update and a box for a current notice. Each service follows with its state in words, an uptime figure and a 30-day bar. The top bar links Status, Maintenance and Previous incidents, and a language menu sits in the footer.
references.apply: Eleva's status page: one sentence on top, when it was last checked, then booking, video sessions, payments and email each with a state in words. Planned maintenance and past incidents are one click away, in EN, PT and ES.
references.query: public status page showing system components and uptime

references.pattern: Maintenance announced ahead in a bar: why, the exact window with its time zone, and what will not work
references.why: A slim bar across the top reads: 'To make PandaDoc faster, we are upgrading our system on Apr 21, 01:00 AM - 05:00 AM PST. During this maintenance window, the PandaDoc application will not be available.' It ends with 'More details' and a close button.
references.apply: Before planned maintenance, show a bar with the date and window in the reader's own time zone and what will not work, and link to the status page. The 'back soon' page repeats the same window and says how to reach Eleva; no Mobbin result showed a full maintenance page.
references.query: scheduled maintenance page saying the service will be back soon

references.pattern: The error stays inside the page: the menu, the title and the filters remain, and the content area says what failed with one 'Try again'
references.why: On Cards, the list did not load. The sidebar, the page title, the search and the two filter chips ('Filters · 1', 'Pending') are all still there. The panel shows a warning icon, 'Connection issue' and one 'Try again' button, and a slim bar on top says 'Back online' once the connection returns.
references.apply: Eleva's dashboard error page renders inside the shell, so the sidebar and the account menu keep working. The content area holds one short title, one or two sentences and 'Try again', which loads the same address again so anything kept in the URL stays. Eleva adds what Revolut leaves out: what to do next, a second way out and a reference.
references.query: dashboard error page with a try again button

references.pattern: An error ID under the message with a copy button, and a line on what to do if it happens again
references.why: The page says something went wrong, that the team has been told, to refresh and, if it goes on, to contact support. 'Refresh' is the one button. Under it, in small grey type: 'Error ID: 3a76…' with a copy icon. Kept for its structure only: the joke about frantic keyboards is not Eleva's voice.
references.apply: Show 'Reference: {code}' in the monospace face with a 'Copy reference' button that has words, and tell the reader to send it to support if the page fails again. Keep the reference next to the message, not at the foot of the page, and confirm the copy in words.
references.query: dashboard error page with a try again button

references.pattern: Two ways on: the main button tries again, a quiet link under it leaves for the dashboard
references.why: 'An error occurred. Please reload the page.' with a 'Reload' button and, under it, a small text link, 'Go to dashboard'. The second action is plainly the lesser one, so the eye goes to the retry first, and there is still a way out when retrying keeps failing.
references.apply: 'Try again' is the only filled button. Beside it sits a quiet link with the same words as the not-found page ('Go to dashboard'). Eleva writes a fuller message than Chronicle: what failed, what to do next and the reference.
references.query: dashboard error page with a try again button

references.pattern: Trust centre with four tabs, and its questions written the way a visitor asks them
references.why: A slim bar under the header reads Trust, then Overview, Security, Privacy and Legal, so the trust centre is one place with four doors. The Security tab ends with questions in the visitor's words ('How do you store my data?', 'What laws do you comply with when it comes to data privacy?') and a short 'Security questions' block with one 'Contact us' button. A design tool, kept for the structure.
references.apply: Group /trust by what the visitor wants to know, not by document: a short anchor bar (Your health information, Security, Experts we check, Documents). Under the fact tiles, answer four or five questions in a member's words, two sentences each, with a link to the document. End the page with one contact block for privacy and security.
references.query: security section of a health app website

references.pattern: One 'TLDR' paragraph above the policy, with searchable contents in a side rail
references.why: Under the title sits one paragraph that starts in bold: 'TLDR: Craft does not own your data, nor do we sell it to others or use it for advertising.' A dotted rule then separates it from the legal text. The left rail lists every section and has a search field, so a reader reaches 'Data Retention' or 'Your Privacy Rights' in one step. A notes product, kept for the layout.
references.apply: Open every policy with an 'In short' block of three to five plain sentences, set apart from the full text by a rule and the line that the full text below is what applies. Eleva's summary says what Eleva does: who sees health information, where it is stored, how long it is kept, and your choices. Summary wording needs legal review.
references.query: privacy policy page with a plain-language summary

references.pattern: Two dates over the title (posted, and in effect) and a link to the previous version
references.why: A small line over the title reads 'Effective as of March 1, 2023 | Posted: December 1, 2022', so a reader sees the change was announced three months before it applied. Directly under the title is '(View Previous Version)'. After two short paragraphs a 'Summary' heading introduces 'a brief overview of some important points'. A writing tool, kept for the dating.
references.apply: Show 'Last updated' on every policy and, when a change is announced ahead, 'In effect from', and link the previous version. Eleva already stores the consent version as a date, so a member can open the exact text she agreed to.
references.query: privacy policy page with a plain-language summary

references.pattern: On a phone: sibling policies as a scrolling tab row, then the dates, then numbered contents as the first screen
references.why: An iOS screen. Under the title a row of tabs (About, Terms & Conditions, Privacy Policy) lets the reader change document without going back. The effective date and the last-updated date come next, and the rest of the first screen is a numbered list of thirteen sections. No legal text shows until the reader picks a section. A fashion retailer, kept for the phone layout.
references.apply: On phones, put 'On this page' directly under the date and the 'In short' block as a numbered list that can be folded, and add a scrolling row of sibling policies so a reader moves from Privacy to Cookies to Health data in one tap. Give each row at least 24px of height.
references.query: privacy policy screen with a short summary and section list

references.pattern: A plain-language layer first: cards that explain the policy, with the full text one link below
references.why: An iOS screen. The Policies page says 'Explore a different kind of privacy policy to understand how your data works for you' and shows cards, each with a drawing, one sentence ('And here's how to be the boss of your data') and 'Learn more'. Under the cards a lock row reads 'Read our full privacy policy'. The short version and the legal version are plainly two layers. A furniture retailer, kept for the layering.
references.apply: Offer the summary as its own layer: three or four cards (what we collect, who sees your health information, how long we keep it, your choices), each linking to its section, then 'Read the full privacy notice'. On Eleva the cards stack on phones instead of scrolling sideways, so nothing sits off screen.
references.query: privacy policy screen with a short summary and section list

references.pattern: An action button directly under the policy title, and 'Who we are' as the first section
references.why: An iOS screen from a Berlin company. The first thing under 'Privacy Policy' is a filled button, 'Manage settings'. The first heading is 'Who we are, and the purpose of this Privacy Policy'; its first sentence names the company and its street address, and the paragraph says it is the controller. A reader can act before reading and knows who is responsible within one screen. A language app, kept for the order.
references.apply: Under each policy title add the action that belongs to it: 'Manage your privacy choices' on the privacy notice, 'Cookie settings' on the cookie policy. Keep 'Who the controller is' as section 1 with the legal name and address in the first line, as Eleva already does.
references.query: privacy policy screen with a short summary and section list

references.pattern: The button to withdraw consent sits inside the policy, under the paragraph that describes the right
references.why: A Berlin company's privacy policy sets out each purpose under the same small headings: nature and purpose, legal basis, recipients, withdrawal of consent. Under 'Withdrawal of Consent' the text says you can withdraw at any time by clicking 'Manage cookie settings' below, and the outlined button is right there. A presentation tool, kept for the structure.
references.apply: In the cookie policy and the privacy notice, place a 'Cookie settings' button where withdrawal is described, and 'Download your data' and 'Delete your account' buttons in 'Your rights'. Use the same sub-headings for each purpose so every section reads the same way.
references.query: cookie consent banner with reject and accept buttons

references.pattern: Each cookie group says what it does in one or two always-visible sentences, with one save button
references.why: The dialog lists Essential, Analytics and Marketing. Under each name one or two grey sentences say what the group does and what it is not used for ('This data is aggregated and not used for advertising'). The Essential switch is on and dimmed, and the intro says 'Essential cookies are always active'. A Cookie Policy link and one 'Save Preferences' button close it. A media tool, kept for the row copy; Eleva keeps its equal 'Reject optional' and 'Accept all' buttons, which this dialog leaves out.
references.apply: Show the description Eleva has already written under each group name without a tap: what essential cookies do, and that 'Newsletter sign-up' shows the Femme Focus form provided by Beehiiv. Write 'Always on' beside the locked switch so its state is not told by colour alone.
references.query: cookie consent banner

references.pattern: One page with two rights, each a short paragraph, the time it takes and one button
references.why: 'Data Vault' has two sections. 'Access Personal Data' says the button requests a copy of all personal data and 'This can take up to 30 days'. 'Erase Personal Data' says which accounts are deleted, what is lost, in bold that it cannot be undone, how long it takes, and what the deletion does not cancel. Each section ends in one labelled button. A learning app, kept for the structure; the mascot drawings are not Eleva's voice.
references.apply: Give 'Your rights' in the privacy notice, and one entry on /trust, the same shape: 'Get a copy of your data' and 'Delete your account', each with two sentences, the time to a reply (one month under the GDPR) and one button to Privacy settings. Say what deleting does to a booked session.
references.query: privacy request form to access or delete personal data

references.pattern: A deletion request for people without an account: one email field inside the help answer
references.why: In the help centre of a Berlin booking marketplace, 'Data and privacy' opens two answers: 'Unsubscribe from marketing emails' and 'Delete account and all personal data'. The second says you can delete your account and personal data at any time, then shows one required field, 'Email address', and a 'Send' button. No sign-in, no reason, no other field. A bot-check badge sits in the corner. A travel marketplace, kept for the form.
references.apply: Add a short request form to 'Your rights' for members who booked as guests: email, the right they want to use (copy, correction, deletion), Send. Confirm on the page with the date and when to expect a reply, and check the address by email before acting. Post it through the API with bot protection.
references.query: privacy request form to access or delete personal data

references.pattern: Newsletter sign-up with one field, one unticked box that names the purpose, and the privacy line apart
references.why: The form asks for an email address only. Under it is an unticked checkbox: 'I agree to receive marketing communications about Legora's products, services, and events and understand that I can unsubscribe at any time.' A separate line links the Privacy Policy, then 'Subscribe'. The consent says what will be sent and how to stop, and is tied to nothing else. A Swedish legal software company, kept for the consent wording.
references.apply: Beside the Femme Focus form, state the consent in Eleva's words: what arrives and how often, that Beehiiv sends it for Eleva, that every email has an unsubscribe link, and a link to the privacy notice. Ask for the email address only. Never tie the newsletter to booking or sign-up.
references.query: newsletter sign-up form with consent text

references.pattern: Company identity as labelled facts: legal name, address, who is responsible, register and number, VAT number
references.why: A Berlin company's legal notice sets its identity out as facts, not as a sentence: the legal name in bold with street, city, country and an email address; then three label-and-value pairs for the managing director, the commercial register with court and number, and the VAT ID. Labels are grey, values bold. A reader finds any one fact in a second. A presentation tool, kept for the block.
references.apply: Add a 'Who runs Eleva' block to /trust and /contact with the same label-and-value layout: legal name (Búzios e Tartarugas, Lda), registered address, NIPC, the ERS registration where it applies, and the privacy, security and support addresses. The footer carries the one-line version.
references.query: footer with company registration number and registered address

references.pattern: A footer column for security and protection, a short legal row, then the registered entity and its regulator in plain paragraphs
references.why: The footer gives security its own column, 'Security & Protection', with five links such as 'How We Protect Your Money' and 'Security Bugs', apart from Help and Company. The legal links are one short row under the logo, beside the country. Below, plain paragraphs name the company, its registration number, the authority that authorises it and the registered address. A bank, kept for the three layers.
references.apply: Split Eleva's fourteen-link Legal column into 'Trust' (Trust and security, Health data, How we check experts, Accessibility, Report a security issue) and a short 'Legal' list (Terms, Privacy, Cookies, Complaints, Electronic complaints book, Cookie settings). Close with one identity sentence: legal name, NIPC, registered address, ERS registration where it applies.
references.query: footer with company registration number and registered address

references.pattern: At the pay step: a security line above the methods, the total with 'VAT included', and the terms and withdrawal information linked under the button
references.why: A Berlin company's payment page. Above the payment methods a lock row says 'Secure Payment. All transactions will be processed over an SSL-encrypted connection.' The order summary ends in one box, 'Total price' with '(VAT included)' beneath. Directly under 'Buy now' one line links the Terms & Conditions and the withdrawal information. The dates and how to cancel are in the summary. A language app, kept for the pay-step facts an EU buyer expects.
references.apply: At Eleva's pay step show the total as one row with the tax note beneath, one lock line beside the button ('Paid securely through Stripe. Eleva never sees your card number.'), and under the button one line linking the Terms of use and the cancellation policy with its dated deadline. Whether a withdrawal statement applies to a dated health session needs legal review.
references.query: booking checkout payment step with secure payment reassurance next to the pay button

references.pattern: Contact page with a two-field form and an address for each purpose, security included
references.why: 'Get in touch' has two fields, the email address and 'How can we help?', and one Submit button. To the right are three labelled addresses: 'Get help', 'Work at Resend' and 'Report security concerns', each with its own email. A visitor with a security report or a plain question sees where to write without reading a paragraph. An email tool on a dark theme, kept for the structure.
references.apply: Keep Eleva's addresses by purpose (support, privacy, legal, security) and add 'Report a concern about an expert or a session' as its own entry. If a form is added, ask for an email and a message only, say that health details are not needed here, and name who reads it and when to expect a reply.
references.query: responsible disclosure page for reporting a security vulnerability

references.pattern: Accessibility statement with a date, its own small menu, and a 'Conformance status' section that names the standard
references.why: The header holds a small menu (Accessibility at Webflow, Statement, Checklist), the title and 'Last updated on May 20th, 2021'. The first section is 'Conformance status': a left column lists the three areas covered, and the text names what was tested (keyboard operability, screen reader support) and links the standard, 'WCAG 2.1 Level AA'. A site builder, kept for the structure.
references.apply: Give Eleva's accessibility statement the same order: last updated, the standard Eleva works to (WCAG 2.2 AA) and how it is tested, what is covered (public site, booking, member Space), and a clear way to tell Eleva when something does not work, with a reply time. The content of the statement needs legal review against the European Accessibility Act.
references.query: accessibility statement page

judging_criteria: Does the health-information consent explain, on the same screen and in one or two plain sentences, what is processed, who sees it and how to withdraw, while staying a separate unticked choice? (09-trust/01, 09-trust/02)

On the screen with the Pay button, at phone width, can you read the dated cancellation deadline, the total as one row, and a line agreeing to the terms, without scrolling away from the button? (09-trust/03)
Does the pay step name the independent expert as the provider of the session and state Eleva's role in booking and payment? (09-trust/04)
Does the expert profile show the professional body and registration number as a checked fact next to the name or the booking CTA, with a one-tap explanation of what Eleva checks? (09-trust/05)
Does the trust centre state at least five specific facts on the page itself before listing any document, and say who runs Eleva? (09-trust/06, 09-trust/12)

Can a member see the current state and date of every consent, change each optional one with a single switch, and follow an export or deletion request through a dated status, with a delete confirmation that names what is erased and what is kept? (09-trust/08, 09-trust/09, 09-trust/10)

Can a reader of any policy page get a short summary, jump between sections on a phone, start a data request from the rights section, and report a concern about an expert in two steps with a reference number? (09-trust/07, 09-trust/11)

Before and during planned maintenance, does Eleva say when it starts and ends in the reader's time zone and what will not work, and does the status page answer whether Eleva is working in one sentence? (09-trust/13, 09-trust/14)

When a signed-in page fails to load, does the menu stay usable, does the page say in plain words what happened and what to do, does 'Try again' load the page again, is there a second way out, and can the reader copy a reference to send to support? (09-trust/15, 09-trust/16, 09-trust/17)

Does the trust centre group its content by what a visitor asks (health information, security, expert checks, documents), answer at least four questions in a member's words on the page, and end with one contact block? (09-trust/18)

Does every policy page open with an 'In short' summary set apart from the legal text, show a last-updated date with a link to the previous version, and name the controller in the first section? (09-trust/19, 09-trust/20, 09-trust/23)

At 390px wide, does a policy page show its contents list within the first two screens, let the reader move to a sibling policy in one tap, and keep every link at least 24px tall? (09-trust/21, 09-trust/22)

Is there a button to act on a right in the place where the right is described (cookie settings, download your data, delete your account), with the time to a reply stated, and a one-field route for people who booked without an account? (09-trust/24, 09-trust/26, 09-trust/27)

In the cookie dialog, can you read what each group does without opening it, is the essential group marked 'Always on' in words, and are reject and accept the same size and style on the first layer? (09-trust/25, 09-trust/08)
Does the newsletter sign-up ask for an email address only, state beside the form what will be sent and how to unsubscribe, and stay separate from any other agreement? (09-trust/28)

Does the footer separate trust links from legal links and state the legal name, registration number and registered address, and does /trust or /contact show the same identity as labelled facts with an address for each purpose? (09-trust/29, 09-trust/30, 09-trust/32)

On the pay screen, can you read the total with its tax note, one payment-security line that names the payment provider, and links to the terms and the cancellation policy, all without scrolling away from the button? (09-trust/31)
Does the accessibility statement show its date, name the standard it works to, list what it covers and give a way to report a barrier? (09-trust/33)
